title: CUDA context preemption overhead: SKU & driver comparison
content:
Summary:
This notes doc captures an investigation into CUDA context creation/destruction and preemption overhead across representative cloud GPU SKUs (NVIDIA A100, H100, and L40S) and multiple driver/CUDA stacks. The motivating problem is intermittent p95/p99 latency spikes in short-lived request workloads (few tokens, many concurrent requests) that reproduce only at scale. The hypothesis tested: frequent CUDA context churn and kernel preemption behavior differ by architecture and driver, causing observable tail amplification under high request churn.

Goals:
- Measure end-to-end request latency and internal CUDA lifecycle timings when serving many short requests concurrently.
- Compare across SKUs (A100, H100, L40S) and driver/CUDA versions (470/11.x, 525/11.x, 535/12.x where available).
- Identify actionable mitigations (persistent contexts, thread/stream reuse, process model changes).

Test harness and workload:
- Workload: synthetic text-generation micro-requests: 16-64 token outputs, average model context 1024, conditioned on a small prompt. Typical request CPU time ~4-8ms, GPU token generation dominated but single-token-per-kernel calls dominate when batch size == 1.
- Orchestration: k8s nodes provisioned with 1 GPU each to avoid multi-GPU interference; each pod runs the serving binary (same container image) and a load-generator (wrk-like harness) drives N concurrent clients where N varies 50->800.
- Measurements collected:
  - HTTP p50/p95/p99 per-request latency
  - Kernel-launch latency distribution (from CUPTI traces)
  - CUDA context create/destroy times (measured using cuCtxCreate/cuCtxDestroy instrumentation and libcudart wrappers)
  - GPU SM utilization and active contexts (nvidia-smi sampling at 100ms)
  - Kernel preemption events and long-running kernel stalls (from vendor counters where available)
- Driver/CUDA matrix tested (representative):
  - Ubuntu 20.04 base image
  - CUDA 11.8 + driver 525 (A100 baseline)
  - CUDA 11.7 + driver 470 (older baseline, A100 legacy)
  - CUDA 12.1 + driver 535 (H100/L40S newer stacks)

Key results (high level):
- Context creation/destruction dominates single-request overhead when the process model spawns ephemeral worker processes for each request. Median context create+destroy was ~3.8ms on A100 with 525 driver, peaking to >12ms on some runs with driver 470. H100 with CUDA 12.1/535 showed improved median (~1.6ms) but occasional spikes to ~20ms tied to kernel preemption backpressure. L40S showed similar medians to H100 but larger variance under heavy concurrent load (likely due to power/clock governor transitions in the cloud SKU).
- Kernel launch latencies (cold vs warm stream): mean launch overhead ~40-120us in warm paths, but when context churn or preemption occurred we observed queued kernel delays on the order of multiple milliseconds. These queued delays correlated strongly with requests that experienced p99 HTTP latency spikes.
- Driver version matters: the older 470-based stacks were more sensitive to rapid cuCtxCreate/cuCtxDestroy churn. Newer drivers (525/535) reduced average create/destroy time but introduced different behavior: under high concurrency the GPU scheduler preempted/resumed kernels more aggressively, which reduced maximum single-kernel blocking time but increased the tail of short-kernel latency distribution due to repeated preemption/resume overhead.

Observations by SKU:
- A100 (Ampere):
  - Stable under baseline loads. When requests were highly concurrent and contexts were ephemeral, tail amplification was primarily due to context create/destroy and host-side queueing (driver serialization).
  - Enabling persistent contexts (process-per-GPU with per-request work queued into streams) reduced p99 by ~3.5x in our tests.
- H100 (Hopper):
  - Lower median context create/destroy times in newer drivers. However, H100's preemption and TLB behavior sometimes introduced larger variance for workloads with many concurrently scheduled short kernels.
  - When using kernel-fused generation kernels (fewer but longer kernels) the tail improved; when generation used many small kernels per token, tail worsened relative to A100.
- L40S (Ada-like / data center variant):
  - Similar to H100 in medians but cloud SKU power management (clock down/up) under bursty sustained load caused spikes in latency correlated with frequency governor transitions. Sampling at 100ms resolution captured these frequency transitions aligning with p99 spikes.

Repro steps (short):
1) Deploy nodes with identical container images and pinned drivers; ensure CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 only.
2) Start serving binary with two modes: a) ephemeral worker per request (baseline), b) persistent worker pool + stream reuse (mitigation).
3) Run load generator at N=200,400,800 concurrent clients for 600s; collect CUPTI traces, nvidia-smi logs, and HTTP traces.
4) Aggregate and compute PTIME (create/destroy), kernel launch latency buckets, and overall HTTP p50/p95/p99.

Mitigations and recommendations:
- Avoid cuCtxCreate/cuCtxDestroy per request: use process-per-GPU or long-lived pool with stream reuse. This gave the single-largest reduction in p99 in every SKU tested.
- Prefer fused kernels that reduce kernel count per generated token when possible; fewer kernel launches makes preemption and launch overhead less impactful on tails.
- For H100, prefer newer driver stacks (>=525/535) but validate behavior under production concurrency—preemption improves fairness but can increase variance for micro-kernel heavy workloads.
- On cloud L40S SKUs, coordinate with infra to pin boost clocks or use instance types with predictable P-states for latency-sensitive tiers. Monitor clock transitions alongside latency.
- As a platform improvement: expose a "persistent-context" runtime option that defaults to true for dedicated tiers; document memory/per-GPU costs.

Open questions / next experiments:
- Quantify tradeoff between persistent-context memory overhead and p99 reduction at scale for multi-model hosts.
- Measure CUDA IPC / multi-process sharing approaches (e.g., NVLink peer, MPS) vs process-per-GPU patterns for efficiency and tail behavior.
- Deeper CUPTI/kernel-level traces to correlate particular kernel types with preemption/resume overhead on H100.

Appendix: quick data snippets (representative)
- A100, driver 525, ephemeral model: HTTP p99 = 1542ms, p95 = 210ms; after persistent-context: p99 = 420ms, p95 = 130ms.
- H100, driver 535, ephemeral: HTTP p99 = 1900ms (spikey), p95 = 240ms; after kernel fusion + persistent: p99 = 480ms, p95 = 120ms.
- L40S, driver 535, ephemeral: p99 = 2200ms with clear alignment to clock governor transitions; persistent-context reduced p99 to 600ms but spikes still observed when SKU scaled down clocks during steady bursts.

Notes for runbook / customer guidance:
- For hosted API short-response paths (PLG/free-tier), enable request-level queuing and limit concurrency per GPU to avoid context churn.
- For Dedicated/Private customers with latency SLOs, recommend defaulting to persistent contexts and pre-warming common models on startup. Include a knob in runtime config and a metric that counts context churn per minute.

Raw artifacts and scripts location:
- Load harness: github.com/redwood-inference/benchmarks/context-churn-harness
- CUPTI trace parser: github.com/redwood-inference/tools/cupti-parser
- Kubernetes job manifests: infra/playbooks/serving/context-churn-jobs.yaml

Acknowledgements: Miguel ran the A100 matrix, Priya validated driver images on L40S, Jonah aggregated the CUPTI traces.

Next steps: consolidate findings into a short RFC for runtime default changes (persistent-context on by default for Dedicated) and schedule a follow-up deep CUPTI trace session for H100 preemption patterns.
